title: Great Inventions · Episode 1
chapters: Spectacles: the invention that extended working lives
The bicycle: a simple machine that changed society

units.t: Great Inventions. Episode one.
In this episode: Spectacles: the invention that extended working lives, Engines: turning fire into motion, How railways invented time zones and The bicycle: a simple machine that changed society.
Part one. Spectacles: the invention that extended working lives.
Nobody knows who invented glasses, and one famous inventor turns out to be a fake.
But this medieval gadget quietly changed what people could do after forty.
Ageing eyes and stones.
Inside your eye, a flexible lens changes shape to focus at different distances.
With age it stiffens, and by the mid forties most people find small print blurs unless held at arm's length.
This is presbyopia, from the Greek for "old eye".
Before spectacles, a scribe, jeweller or weaver could see their working life cut short at the peak of their skill.
The magnifying power of curved glass was known early.
The Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham studied optics around the year 1000, and his work was later translated into Latin.
Medieval readers used "reading stones", rounded glass or rock crystal laid on the page.
They helped, but you had to slide them along the line, and they were no use for sewing or carving.
Italy, and a fake inventor.
The best early evidence is a sermon.

In 1306 the Dominican friar Giordano da Pisa told a Florentine congregation that eyeglasses had been invented less than twenty years earlier, and that he had met the maker, but he did not record the name.
That points to northern Italy in the 1280s, where Venice had skilled glassworkers.
The first spectacles had two convex lenses, thicker in the middle, in riveted frames perched on the nose.
Many books once named Salvino degli Armati of Florence as the inventor.
The evidence was a tomb inscription, which historians concluded was a seventeenth-century fabrication meant to give Florence the credit.
No reliable earlier record exists.
A satisfying story with a name and a plaque can travel for centuries, even when the honest answer is that we do not know.
Short sight and Kepler.
The first spectacles helped with close work, which is why they spread among older readers.
Short-sighted people, who struggle with distant objects, needed concave lenses, thinner in the middle, which spread light out before it enters the eye.
Clear evidence of these appears by the fifteenth century.
Spectacle makers worked largely by trial and error.

A proper theory came in 1604, when the astronomer Johannes Kepler showed that the eye forms an image on the retina at the back, and that spectacles work by shifting where light comes to a focus so it lands on the retina properly.
Lens makers' skills also fed directly into the invention of the telescope and microscope.
Arms, bifocals, contacts.
For centuries, the hardest part of wearing glasses was keeping them on.
People tried ribbons, leather straps and frames that pinched the nose.
Rigid side arms resting on the ears became common in the eighteenth century, and the London optician Edward Scarlett is often credited with popularising them in the first half of the 1700s.
Benjamin Franklin, tired of swapping between two pairs, described his "double spectacles" in a 1784 letter, with each lens split into a top half for distance and a bottom half for reading.
These became known as bifocals.
In 1888 the German doctor Adolf Fick described glass lenses placed directly on the eye.
Comfortable soft contact lenses arrived in the 1960s, thanks to the Czech chemist Otto Wichterle.
A quiet revolution.
It is easy to overlook glasses because they are everywhere, but their effect has been enormous.
In medieval and early modern Europe, they let scholars, clerks, merchants and craftspeople keep doing detailed work for decades longer.
Some historians argue this gave a small but real boost to learning and productivity, especially after the printing press made books cheaper and reading more common.
The need is still huge.

The World Health Organization estimates that around a billion people worldwide have vision impairment that could have been prevented or has yet to be addressed, much of it simple short sight or presbyopia.
A cheap pair of reading glasses can still keep someone working, reading and independent, just as it did seven centuries ago.
The key idea: From the mid forties the eye's lens stiffens and close focus fails, which reading stones only partly solved before spectacles.
Part two. Engines: turning fire into motion.
For most of history, all power came from muscle, wind and water.
Then people learned to turn fire into motion, and the world sped up.
Pumping out the mines.
For most of history, work was done by the muscles of people and animals, helped by wind and flowing water.
Both depended on where rivers ran and which way the wind blew.
Hero of Alexandria described a steam-spun ball, the aeolipile, in the first century AD, but it was a curiosity.
Turning heat into useful motion took another 1,600 years, and the push came from flooded mines.
Thomas Savery patented a steam pump in 1698, but it was limited and failure-prone.
In 1712 Devon ironmonger Thomas Newcomen built a working engine near Dudley.
Steam filled a cylinder, then a cold spray condensed it, creating a partial vacuum.
Air pressure pushed the piston down to work a pump beam.
Newcomen engines were slow and burned huge amounts of coal, but hundreds were built.
What James Watt really did.
James Watt is often called the inventor of the steam engine, but he improved an existing one.
In 1765, after repairing a model Newcomen engine at the University of Glasgow, he realised it wasted most of its fuel reheating a cylinder that was cooled on every stroke.
His fix was a separate condenser, so the cylinder could stay hot.
Watt and his partner Matthew Boulton sold engines that used roughly a quarter of the coal of a Newcomen engine.
Watt later adapted engines to turn wheels, and coined 'horsepower' to market them.
The popular tale of a boiling kettle inspiring him is a legend.
Steam changes the world.
Steam became a driving force of the Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain around the 1760s.
Factories no longer had to sit beside rivers, so they grew in towns near coal and workers.
In 1804 Richard Trevithick ran the first steam locomotive on rails, in Wales.
In 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, the first intercity line worked entirely by steam locomotives.
Steamships soon crossed oceans regardless of the wind.
Australia's first steam railway opened in Melbourne in 1854, running from Flinders Street to Sandridge, now Port Melbourne.
Journeys that once took days shrank to hours.
Petrol, diesel and the car.
A steam engine burns fuel outside the cylinder to boil water.
An internal combustion engine burns fuel inside it, so it can be smaller and lighter.
Etienne Lenoir built a working gas engine in France around 1860.
In 1876 Nicolaus Otto built a successful four-stroke engine, intake, compression, power, exhaust, a cycle most car engines still use.
In the 1890s Rudolf Diesel developed an engine that ignites fuel simply by squeezing air until it is very hot.
Karl Benz built the first practical petrol car in 1885, patented in 1886.
In 1888 his wife Bertha proved it on real roads, driving about 100 kilometres to visit her mother.
Henry Ford didn't invent the car; he made it cheap, with the Model T in 1908 and his moving assembly line from 1913.
Electric motors, shared credit.
Electric motors turn electricity into motion using magnetism.
In 1821 Michael Faraday showed that a current-carrying wire could rotate around a magnet, the principle behind every motor.
In the late 1880s Nikola Tesla and, independently, Galileo Ferraris developed the AC induction motor, still the workhorse of industry.
Electric cars were fairly common around 1900 before cheap petrol won out.
Electric motors turn around 90 per cent of their energy into motion, while petrol engines manage roughly 20 to 35 per cent.
Big inventions are rarely one person's flash of genius.
Newcomen built on Savery, Watt on Newcomen, and Benz and Diesel on Lenoir and Otto.
Names stick to whoever made an idea practical or profitable.
Engines also brought air pollution and the rise in carbon dioxide behind climate change.
The key idea: Before engines, work ran on muscle, wind and water, and the first practical steam engine of 1712 was built to pump water from flooded mines.
Part three. How railways invented time zones.
Once every town set its clocks by its own sun.
Then trains arrived, timetables turned into chaos, and the world had to agree on what time it was.
Trains break local time.
For most of history, time was local.
Noon was when the Sun stood highest, and because the Earth turns, that moment arrives later the further west you go.
Bristol's clocks ran about ten minutes behind London's.
By horse and coach, nobody cared.
Railways changed the scale.
People covered in hours what once took days, and timetables had to be precise to the minute.
With every station on local time, passengers missed connections, and on single track lines confusion over time could cause collisions.
The telegraph made a solution possible, because a time signal could travel along wires almost instantly.
Railway companies became the keepers of the clock and ran their whole networks on one standard time.
Railway time.
In Britain, the Great Western Railway adopted London time in 1840, and by about 1848 most railways used Greenwich Mean Time.
Some towns kept two times for a while, with public clocks given two minute hands.
In 1880 Parliament made GMT the legal time across Great Britain.
North America had a bigger problem: dozens of railway times, with big stations showing several clocks.
On 18 November 1883 the railways of the United States and Canada switched to standard time zones about an hour apart.
In many towns clocks were reset at noon, so people lived through noon twice, which is why it is remembered as the day of two noons.
The railways, not the government, organised it.
US federal law made time zones official only in 1918.
Choosing Greenwich.
Standard zones need a starting point.
In 1884 delegates from about twenty five countries met in Washington DC for the International Meridian Conference.
They chose the meridian through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich as zero degrees longitude.
Practical reasons favoured it, as most of the world's shipping already used charts based on Greenwich.
The Canadian railway engineer Sandford Fleming was one of the great champions of a worldwide system of time based on a single meridian.
Not everyone agreed: France abstained in the vote and kept using the Paris meridian for its own purposes for decades.
The conference did not impose time zones around the world, but it gave countries a shared reference to build their own on.
Australia's time zones.
In Australia, each colony had kept its own local time, and travellers crossing borders by train faced the same headaches as everyone else.
In 1895 the colonies agreed on standard times based on Greenwich: Eastern, Central and Western.
South Australia first chose nine hours ahead of Greenwich, but in 1899 moved to nine and a half hours, a choice that has been debated ever since.
The Northern Territory, then administered by South Australia, followed.
Half-hour zones are unusual but not unique: India uses one, and Nepal goes further with a quarter-hour offset.
Daylight saving complicates things today.
Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory don't use it, so in summer the mainland runs on five different times.
Time today.
Greenwich Mean Time has largely been replaced as the world's reference by Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, kept by a network of highly accurate atomic clocks.
Because the Earth's spin is slightly irregular, leap seconds have occasionally been added to keep UTC close to the Sun, but in 2022 international scientists voted to stop adding them by 2035.
Time zones themselves are decided by governments, and politics often beats geography.
China, which spans the width of five standard zones, uses just one official time, so in its far west the Sun can rise very late by the clock.
Spain sits mostly west of Greenwich but uses Central European Time.
The railway engineers' solution still governs every phone and laptop.
The key idea: Each town once kept its own solar noon, and fast trains with precise timetables made that confusing and dangerous.
Part four. The bicycle: a simple machine that changed society.
Two wheels, a frame and a chain.
The bicycle looks so obvious it is hard to believe it took the best part of a century to get right, or that it helped change the lives of women.
A running machine.
In 1817, German forestry official Karl Drais rode a strange new machine near Mannheim.
It had two wheels in a line, a wooden frame and a seat, and he pushed it along by striding with his feet on the ground, much like a modern children's balance bike.
He called it a Laufmaschine, or running machine.
It became known as the draisine or dandy horse.
Some historians link the invention to 1816, the Year Without a Summer, when a huge volcanic eruption in Indonesia had disrupted the climate.
Crop failures made feeding horses expensive.
The dandy horse craze faded quickly, but the idea of balancing on two wheels had arrived.
Boneshakers and high wheelers.
In the 1860s in France, makers attached pedals and cranks directly to the front wheel, so riders could lift their feet off the ground.
Credit is disputed between the Michaux family business in Paris and a mechanic named Pierre Lallement.
These velocipedes had iron frames and wooden wheels with iron rims, and on rough roads they rattled so badly they were nicknamed boneshakers.
They were still popular, with riding schools and races.
With pedals fixed to the front wheel, each turn moved the bike only as far as its circumference.
So makers enlarged the wheel.
By the 1870s, high wheelers had front wheels well over a metre across, later nicknamed penny-farthings.
Solid rubber tyres and wire spokes made them light and fast, but hitting a rock or pothole could pitch the rider head first over the handlebars.
The safety bicycle.
The breakthrough came in 1885, when English inventor John Kemp Starley launched the Rover.
It had two wheels of similar size and a chain driving the back wheel.
Gearing in the chain drive meant a small wheel could still travel fast, and the rider sat low enough to put a foot down.
It was called a safety bicycle, and its basic layout is still used today.
Comfort followed.
In 1888, John Boyd Dunlop, a Scottish vet living in Belfast, developed an air-filled tyre for his young son's tricycle.
Pneumatic tyres made riding far smoother and faster, and Dunlop's name became a famous brand.
By the 1890s, the modern bicycle was essentially complete.
Freedom on two wheels.
The 1890s bicycle craze reached far beyond transport.
For many women, the bicycle meant travelling without a chaperone or a horse and carriage.
It also encouraged dress reform: long skirts and tight corsets were impractical, so some women adopted divided skirts or bloomers, to critics' outrage.
In 1896 American campaigner Susan B. Anthony said the bicycle had done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world.
Australia caught the craze too.
Cyclists carried mail across the Western Australian goldfields, shearers rode between stations, and some rode around the continent.
Bikes were cheaper than horses and needed no feed or water, a big advantage in dry country.
Hubert Opperman became a hero for endurance riding in the 1920s and 1930s, and in 1990 Victoria became the first place in the world to make bicycle helmets compulsory.
Small machine, big legacy.
The bicycle's influence spread into other machines.
Makers developed and refined ball bearings, chain drives, pneumatic tyres and lightweight steel tubing, all of which fed into early cars and motorcycles.
In some countries the campaign for better roads began with cyclists, before motorists took it over.
Most famously, Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, and used its skills, tools and profits to build the aeroplane they flew in 1903.
Today the bicycle remains one of the most energy-efficient ways for a person to travel.
In cities from Amsterdam to Copenhagen, bikes are used for a large share of daily trips, and cities around the world are building bike lanes to follow their lead.
The key idea: The first two-wheeler, built by Karl Drais in 1817, had no pedals and was pushed along with the feet.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did spectacles matter so much to skilled workers?
Answer. Ageing eyes lose close focus; glasses restored working years.
Question two. What problem drove the invention of the first practical steam engines?
Answer. Deep mines filling with water.
Question three. Why did local solar time become a problem?
Answer. Fast trains and timetables made differing town times unsafe.
Question four. How did riders move Karl Drais's 1817 machine?
Answer. By striding along the ground.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
